passage:
14 March, late
Tejas asked at dinner why we say grace when the farmers did all the work. Anita went still. I felt my neck get hot. My own father would have sent me from the table for that. I nearly said, "Because we do," and heard how thin it sounded before it left my mouth. So I asked him what he thought grace was for. He talked for ten minutes: gratitude, the farmers, whether God needs thanks at all. Some of it stung. Some of it was better than anything I could have said at fifteen. I am still unsettled tonight. But he kept talking, and he cleared the plates without being asked. Maybe tomorrow we will thank the farmers by name.
Francis

qa.q: What did Tejas ask at dinner?
qa.a: Tejas asked why we say grace when the farmers did all the work.

qa.q: How can you tell Francis felt unsettled by the question?
qa.a: Francis's neck got hot, the words "Because we do" nearly came out, and even late that night Francis writes of still being unsettled.

qa.q: What choice did Francis make at the key moment, and what followed?
qa.a: Francis asked Tejas what grace was for instead of shutting him down, and Tejas kept talking and even cleared the plates.

qa.q: How might Tejas have felt when his question was taken seriously?
qa.a: He probably felt respected rather than in trouble, which may be why he kept talking and helped clear up.

grounding: A parent is shaken when a curious teenager questions a family custom at dinner, feels both unease and pride, and listens first.

passage:
Late that night, Santosh texted his mother from his room.
Santosh: sorry if I was rude at dinner
Devika (Mum): You weren't rude. You asked why we touch the feet of relatives we barely know.
Devika (Mum): I didn't have a quick answer, and that rattled me a bit.
Santosh: so you're angry
Devika (Mum): No. Unsettled. And honestly a little proud. You think things through.
Santosh: I just don't get bowing to someone I met once
Devika (Mum): Tell me more. What would feel real to you instead?
Santosh: maybe saying namaste and actually talking to them?
Devika (Mum): Worth trying at Sunday lunch. And I'll tell you why Ammamma cares about it so much.
Santosh: ok. deal 🙂
Devika (Mum): Goodnight, beta.

qa.q: What did Santosh ask about at dinner?
qa.a: He asked why we touch the feet of relatives we barely know.

qa.q: What mix of feelings does Devika describe about the dinner question?
qa.a: She felt unsettled and a little proud at once: rattled at having no quick answer, but glad he thinks things through.

qa.q: What choice did Devika make when Santosh asked if she was angry?
qa.a: She named her real feelings and asked what would feel real to him, which kept him talking and led to a plan for Sunday.

qa.q: What might it be like for Santosh to send that first message after dinner?
qa.a: He seems worried he crossed a line; finding his mother curious rather than angry lets him relax and agree to the plan.

grounding: A mother feels unsettled and proud when her son questions a family custom, and keeps the talk open by listening first.

passage: Pradeep had twelve minutes before the night bus to the depot, and his dal was still too hot to eat fast. That was when Siddharth, fifteen, put down his spoon. 'Papa, why do we fast on Ekadashi? If God is everywhere, why would God want us hungry?' Pradeep's first thought was to snap that some things aren't questioned. His second was of his own father, who had never let him ask anything. He blew on the dal. 'What's made you think about it?' Siddharth talked fast: a book from the school library, a friend who fasts in Ramzan, a video about why people fast at all. Pradeep checked the clock and felt his chest tighten, and something else too, something like pride. 'I have to go. Sunday, you and me, tea and this question. Keep the book for me.'

qa.q: How long did Pradeep have before the night bus?
qa.a: Twelve minutes.

qa.q: What mix of feelings did Pradeep have as Siddharth talked?
qa.a: He felt uneasy, his chest tightening at a custom being questioned, but also proud of how Siddharth was thinking.

qa.q: Why did asking 'What's made you think about it?' work better than snapping?
qa.a: It let Siddharth explain his reasons and kept him talking, leaving the door open for Sunday instead of shutting the topic.

qa.q: What is it like for Siddharth when Papa asks a question instead of snapping?
qa.a: Siddharth feels safe enough to pour out what he has been reading, and may trust Papa more with hard questions.

grounding: Shows a parent short of time who is unsettled when his teenager questions a family practice at dinner, feels worry and pride together, and listens first.

passage: 'Why is it a duty, though?' Varun asked, halfway through the rotis. 'You say I'll run the shop because Dada ran it. That's not a reason, it's a history.' Sumit felt the words land somewhere under his ribs. Thirty years behind that counter in Lajpat Nagar, and his son had just called it history. His wife glanced at him. He wanted to say, 'Because I said so.' Instead he put his roti down. 'All right. Tell me what you'd want instead.' Varun blinked, as if he'd been ready for a fight. He talked about design, about fabrics he'd seen online, about a course in Ahmedabad. Sumit listened, worried about the shop, and quietly astonished at how well the boy argued. 'Come to the shop after school tomorrow,' he said. 'Show me what you mean.'

qa.q: Where is the family shop?
qa.a: In Lajpat Nagar.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling when Varun called the shop 'a history'?
qa.a: He felt hurt and unsettled, the words landing under his ribs, and worried about what would become of the shop.

qa.q: What did Sumit's choice to listen first make possible?
qa.a: Varun talked instead of fighting, Sumit heard about the design idea, and they agreed to meet at the shop the next day.

qa.q: Why might Varun have blinked when Sumit asked what he'd want?
qa.a: Varun expected an argument or a flat no, so being asked was surprising and probably a relief.

grounding: Shows a parent unsettled when his teenager challenges a long-held family expectation at dinner, feeling worry and pride together, and choosing to listen first.

passage:
'Papa, do you actually believe in rebirth?'
Kamal paused with the pickle jar. 'Why?'
'We learned how memory works in biology. If memories are in the brain, what's left to be reborn?'
'Your Dadi believed it all her life.'
'I know. I'm not saying she was wrong. I'm asking what you think.'
Kamal set the jar down. Nobody had asked him that. Not even himself, not in years.
'I can't argue it like your biology teacher,' he said slowly. 'But tell me the whole thing. Properly.'
'Seriously?'
'Seriously. Then I'll tell you why Dadi believed it, and you can argue with that too.'
Yash grinned. 'Deal.'
Kamal's stomach was still tight. But the boy was thinking. That, he had to admit, felt good.

qa.q: What had Yash learned about in biology?
qa.a: How memory works.

qa.q: Why was Kamal's stomach still tight even as he agreed to listen?
qa.a: He felt unsettled that a belief his mother held all her life was being questioned, while quietly proud that the boy was thinking.

qa.q: What did Kamal's 'tell me the whole thing' do for their talk?
qa.a: It turned a possible fight into an exchange, where Yash explains and then hears why Dadi believed, keeping the door open.

qa.q: What might Yash feel when Papa says 'Seriously'?
qa.a: Yash seems surprised and pleased, grinning, glad to be taken seriously instead of told off.

grounding: Shows a parent unsettled when his teenager questions a family belief at the table, feeling both anxiety and pride, and choosing to listen first.

passage: Last Karva Chauth, my daughter Mehak, sixteen, put down her spoon and asked her mother, "Why do only women fast for their husbands? Why doesn't Papa fast for you?" I'm Yogesh, her father, and I felt the room tilt. My first urge was to say, "Because that's how it is." My chest felt tight; I worried she was throwing away everything we'd taught her. But I also felt a strange pride. It was a sharp question. So I didn't answer straight away. I asked, "What makes you ask?" She talked for twenty minutes about fairness. I listened. At the end I said, "I don't have a perfect answer. Maybe I'll fast next year too." She laughed. Now she brings her questions to me first.

qa.q: On which occasion did Mehak ask her question?
qa.a: On Karva Chauth, at dinner.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel when Mehak asked why only women fast?
qa.a: He felt unsettled and anxious, his chest tight, but also proud of her sharp question.

qa.q: What did Yogesh do that kept the door open?
qa.a: He listened first by asking what made her ask, heard her out for twenty minutes and admitted he didn't have a perfect answer.

qa.q: How might Mehak see her father now?
qa.a: Mehak seems to see him as someone safe to question, since she now brings her questions to him first.

grounding: Shows a parent unsettled when his teenager questions a long-held custom, feeling both anxiety and pride, and choosing to listen first.
